mappings.note: The rope runs along the boundary only, and the distractor 1350 m is the AREA 45x30. The item exists to separate perimeter from area, which is C-7.1-LO-1.
Two gardens of equal perimeter 40 m whose areas differ -- C-7.1-LO-1's 'produces two figures of equal perimeter whose areas differ', put as a comparison.
One lap of a circular track is the circumference 2 pi r. LO-2 of C-7.3 owns the circumference relation; LO-3 would apply only to part of the circle.
Inverts C = 2 pi r to test a claimed radius, catching the student who divided by 2 without pi. C-7.3-LO-2.

The semicircular arc is correctly computed as pi r (LO-3 of C-7.3, the half-circle case), but the boundary of the region also needs the diameter -- a perimeter-of-a-composite-boundary point, C-7.1-LO-1.
Arc length of a 90 degree sector from radius 14. C-7.3-LO-3 verbatim; the area of the sector is not asked, so not LO-4.
15 minutes is a quarter turn, so the swept region is a quarter-circle: sector AREA, which is LO-4's extension. LO-3 would give the arc the tip travels, not the region swept.
Area of a parallelogram depends only on base and perpendicular height, not on the slant side. That invariance is the content of C-7.3-LO-1's derivation from the rectangle.
A parallelogram and a rectangle on the same base and of the same height have equal area -- exactly the equivalence C-7.3-LO-1 establishes.
The contractor computed base times height and forgot the half. C-5.1-LO-1, the base-and-height area of a triangle; no side lengths are given, so Heron (LO-2) does not arise.
The semi-perimeter is the first step of Heron's formula and the student doubled instead of halving. C-5.1-LO-2.
Equal areas, unequal perimeters -- the converse pairing to the equal-perimeter item, and the same C-7.1-LO-1 distinction between the two measures.

Goal-level: plain rectangle area, length fixed, solve for the new breadth. No outcome in this chapter covers the area of a rectangle on its own -- LO-5 of C-5.1 is for composite figures and C-7.3-LO-1 derives the parallelogram FROM the rectangle -- so CG-5's 'uses formulae to calculate areas of plane figures' is the honest level.
Distance per revolution is the circumference pi d, multiplied by 100 and converted to metres. C-7.3-LO-2.
Circumference is a fixed multiple of the radius, so the ratio is preserved -- the constancy of the ratio is precisely what C-7.3-LO-2 establishes. The 25:16 distractor is the area answer.
Doubling r quadruples pi r squared. A property of the circle's AREA, C-7.3-LO-4, and the reason the circumference item above behaves differently.
Four side lengths do not fix a quadrilateral's area unless it is cyclic, which is the condition Brahmagupta's formula needs. C-5.1-LO-3.

Staggered starts exist because outer lanes have longer curved arcs at the same central angle -- arc length (LO-3) resting on the circumference relation (LO-2). Heron and the triangle areas are the distractors.
The reason argues from Heron's formula that scaling every side by k scales s and each (s-a) by k, so the area scales by k squared. C-5.1-LO-2 used structurally rather than numerically.

The hexagon is decomposed into six equilateral triangles, which is LO-5's splitting of a composite figure, and both areas are then compared against pi r squared (C-7.3-LO-4). (The printed explanation contradicts its own verdict; see the defect list.)
Edging runs round the boundary, so the quantity needed is the circumference 2 pi r before any costing. C-7.3-LO-2.
Same circumference-then-cost structure as the previous item, with r = 3.5 chosen so that 2 pi r is exactly 22 m. C-7.3-LO-2.
Painting a disc needs pi r squared, the circle's AREA. C-7.3-LO-4, and the contrast with the edging items above is the point of having both.
Rotations to cover 1 km is total distance divided by the circumference, with a rounding-up judgement at the end. C-7.3-LO-2.
Doubling the radius quadruples the area, refuting the 'twice' claim. C-7.3-LO-4; the same misconception as the logo item but set in a comparison.
Six rectangles of perimeter 24 cm with areas from 11 to 36 -- a systematic demonstration that equal perimeter does not fix area, which is C-7.1-LO-1.
Goal-level: floor area, tile area and a division, with a cm-to-m conversion as the real difficulty. Rectangle area has no outcome of its own in this frame, as with the farmer's field item.
Why a square of equal area to a rectangle can be constructed, and what the two must share. C-7.1-LO-2's construction and its justification, asked as the reasoning rather than the drawing.
Reasons from half(a+b)h without computing either area. A trapezium is the composite figure LO-5 covers, and the argument is that equal a+b and equal h force equal area.

Four semicircles of radius a/2 total pi a squared over 2, compared with the square's a squared. The semicircle areas are C-7.3-LO-4; assembling them against the square is the composite reasoning of C-5.1-LO-5.
The construction asked for is a median, justified by equal bases and a shared height. C-5.1-LO-4 verbatim; the given perimeter of 36 m is a red herring.

Asks for the area AND the perimeter of each half, and then a fencing total that adds an internal dividing line to the outer boundary. Holding the two measures apart is what the item tests, C-7.1-LO-1.
The cut removes area but leaves the perimeter unchanged, which is the C-7.1-LO-1 point; getting the remaining area needs the L-shape treated as a composite figure, C-5.1-LO-5.
A fixed 40 m of fencing, several rectangles, and the observation that the square maximises the area. C-7.1-LO-1's equal-perimeter-different-area outcome, as an investigation.

Competency plus outcome: part 1 is the chord-and-tangent theorem that a perpendicular from the centre bisects a chord, which is C-7.3's circle-theorem clause and has no outcome of its own here; the later parts work with the two radii and the annulus, which is C-7.3-LO-4's circle area.

Part 1 rewrites the semicircle's area in terms of its diameter (LO-4) and part 2 compares the curved ARC lengths of the three semicircles (LO-3). The item turns on areas scaling quadratically while arcs scale linearly.
Defines the perimeter as the total boundary length. The first half of C-7.1-LO-1's distinction.
Why one is measured in length units and the other in square units -- the dimensional side of the perimeter/area distinction, C-7.1-LO-1.
Asks explicitly for an example where one changes while the other does not. C-7.1-LO-1's second clause.
The assertion that equal perimeter forces equal area is false, and the counterexample is what C-7.1-LO-1 requires students to produce.
The maximum-area rectangle for a fixed perimeter, investigated by tabulation. C-7.1-LO-1 pushed to a conclusion, at five marks.
States C = 2 pi r. C-7.3-LO-2, which names the constant ratio and hence this formula.
Circumference of a radius-7 circle with pi as 22/7. Direct use of C-7.3-LO-2's relation.
Circumference proportional to radius because 2 pi is a constant -- the proportionality that C-7.3-LO-2 establishes.
True/false recall of C = 2 pi r. C-7.3-LO-2.
Solves 176 = 2 pi r for the radius. C-7.3-LO-2 inverted.
States pi r squared. C-7.3-LO-4 is the outcome that derives the circle's area; LO-2 covers only the circumference.
Area of a radius-7 circle. Direct use of C-7.3-LO-4's formula, and the numerical partner of qid:706753.
False: doubling r quadruples the area, because the radius is squared. C-7.3-LO-4, with the true reason failing to support the assertion.
Trebling r multiplies the area by nine. Same quadratic-scaling point as qid:706759, in true/false form.
Gap-fill for pi r squared. C-7.3-LO-4.

An inventory of perimeter and area formulae across rectangle, square, triangle and circle (CG-5's 'derives and uses formulae for areas of plane figures'), with the units of each, which is C-7.1-LO-1's dimensional distinction.
The triangle row is C-5.1-LO-1 and the circle row is C-7.3-LO-4; the square and rectangle rows have no outcome of their own, so CG-5 carries them.
Half base times height with base 10 and height 6. C-5.1-LO-1.

The proof is by copying and rotating the triangle to make a parallelogram, which is C-7.3-LO-1's 'triangle as half that of a parallelogram'. C-5.1-LO-1 is the formula being justified, not the justification.
Equal areas on the same base between the same parallels -- the second clause of C-7.3-LO-1, stated as a true/false.
Another base-and-height area computation. C-5.1-LO-1; cited to the formula outcome rather than to the derivation outcome because no reasoning is asked for.
The full proof that triangles on the same base between the same parallels are equal in area, via the shared perpendicular height. C-7.3-LO-1, at five marks.
Defines pi as the circumference-to-diameter ratio -- C-7.3-LO-2's 'names that ratio pi'. Not C-7.1-LO-3, which is about its irrationality.
False: the ratio is the same for every circle, which is the whole content of C-7.3-LO-2's 'every circle bears the same ratio'.
